doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Ben Webster, train trips and coffee in Copenhagen
summary: Ben Webster would not fly, so Johnstone traveled with him, heard stories about Lester Young, and had coffee at his place; the Copenhagen scene raised everyone's level.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: And it was magical because he would engage the audience to understand the story he was telling, and then play it. And you could feel it the whole way. And the sound, just the clarity of sound. Everything was solid from the bottom of the horn to the top of the horn. There were no — nothing sounded strained, and which was something I’d always heard with baritone players, the top end was always, you know, you’re dragging it up with your lip. And so I watched him a lot as he was doing it, and he was really, really relaxed. And so I thought well I’ll just put the Dexter Gordon thing in my head. And when I played the clarity came. And so that was some really, really valuable stuff that I was getting from those guys. And Ben Webster was also another one who, because he wouldn’t fly, the Copenhagen Radio Orchestra would send me out with him so we’d ride trains and buses and boats and things to get to the gigs. And he would just sit around and talk to me. And he’d tell me about how Lester Young’s mother used to make them sandwiches before he and Lester went down swimming. You know, just real stuff. And I thought he was just a charming guy. He also made the best coffee in Copenhagen.
He told me, “hey, you want to come over for coffee?” I’d zoom over and we’d sit and chat and play a little.
You can’t buy that kind of stuff.

I know, I know. And I just feel really, really fortunate that I was able to stumble into this. Because of their influence in Copenhagen, players there moved up to their level. And when you hear somebody who can really play, you want to come up to their level and so I was doing that, the bass players and drummers and pianists all were trying to do that. And the legacy of what those guys left after they passed is still really solid in Denmark.
